speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Deniger) on a point of order.
Summer Recess

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext: Would the Leader of the Opposition allow me one or two questions so that I may properly understand his rationale and the conclusions he suggests to the House?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: With the consent of the Leader of the Opposition.
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did appreciate the comments of the Leader of the Opposition. I think he eloquently made a very strong case about the specific impact of a postal strike on the Canadian people. He mentioned some particular cases and rightly so, and many more could be added. However, does the Leader of the Opposition think that the right to strike should be taken away from postal workers? If not, does the Leader of the Opposition think that we should immediately legislate them back to work?

I want to answer very briefly, Mr. Speaker. I think it would be a mistake to take away the right to strike from postal workers. The hon. member will remember that we have suggested another way of settling disputes in the public sector. I hope this government will be prepared to implement such a solution. But, at least until we have a more efficient mechanism, we must respect the right of the workers to strike, and we must also recognize the right of Parliament to act in case of emergency to provide services. Back to work legislation immediately? Of course not. If, as I often said, we can reach a negotiated settlement, that would be a lot better. But the government must show evidence that it is really determined to reach such a settlement by negotiation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. Leader of the Opposition allow a supplementary question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I share many of the feelings which were expressed by the Leader of the Opposition, but I would like to get things clear. The motion put forward by our House leader does provide that at any time prior to that date if the government becomes convinced that the public interest requires that the House should meet at an earlier time, Madam Speaker may give notice that she is so satisfied and thereupon the House shall meet in due time. Therefore, does the Leader of the Opposition not agree that the guarantee which he is seeking can be found in the notice of motion introduced by the Government House leader?

With this motion, the government alone is deciding what the public interest requires. We have no confidence in the government to make such a decision. It is for Parliament to make that judgment. We are here and we intend to stay here to allow Parliament, not just the government, to decide what the public interest, the Canadian interest requires. We consider bankruptcies, problems affecting individuals,
11438

July 10, 1981
Summer Recess
people losing their jobs, as a serious situation and a threat to public interest. We do not want to leave Ottawa and let the government decide on a matter of public interest, when we feel that Parliament is a much better judge of the matter than the government.

Mr. Speaker, I rise not to speak in this debate, but on a point of order. There are certain discussions taking place this afternoon in which my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa is involved which, we dare to hope, might be fruitful. I believe the Leader of the Opposition has been informed of these discussions. Because they are taking place, we feel it would be better not to speak at this time. I should like to reserve my right to speak later in the debate, if it goes on.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak as one individual member of Parliament this afternoon and say that I am appalled at the government's attitude that this Parliament should rise for a three-month holiday, that this Parliament should walk away while the country remains in the grip of a strike which is so badly hurting the Canadian people. I find it unconscionable that the Liberal government should propose that we leave countless thousands of Canadians in a situation where they are deprived of a service that so many people depend upon for their livelihood, their jobs, their pay cheques and the welfare of their families.
How could a Government of Canada possibly be so insensitive to the welfare of so many Canadians? How could the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) make such an unbelievable statement as he did on Monday of this week when he said that he did not want his government to legislate the postal workers back to their jobs because he did not think the postal workers would obey that order?
I want to read into the record a commentary from a former colleague of mine in the parliamentary press gallery who is now a reporter on CFRA, Mr. Hal Anthony. On July 7 he said:
Canadians reached a plateau of sorts yesterday. They were told by their Prime Minister that the government will not introduce a certain piece of legislation because it wouldn't be obeyed.
The elected representatives of the people are running scared, afraid of a powerful and determined union.
The possibility of levying heavy fines seems to have escaped the government. The thought of sending postal union leaders to jail is enough to paralyse the Canadian government. If the government were to stand on a principle and say, "Having given the posties the right to strike we cannot now forbid a strike," one could understand that. But no, the Canadian government quite clearly is caving in to blackmail. The private and public sectors are already shuddering about their own union contracts should the posties win the day. They cannot be allowed to win all they are asking for... that's clear to just about everybody except organized labour. But the government is ducking the issue and uncounted thousands of Canadians will pay the price. The anguish and economic hardship is being felt across the land, but the government backs away, fearful of enacting a law it doesn't want to enforce. It's a sorry day for Canada, and for all of us.
We could not agree more with our leader that we as parliamentarians simply cannot walk away from an issue that this government may want to run away from but that the people want brought to a dead halt.
I do not like to face the prospect of going back to my constituents and telling them that I as a member on this side of the House or, indeed, a member of Parliament on any side of the House, did not do the best we could; that we in the official opposition did not do the best we could to convince the government to be sensible for once, to public opinion and to listen to this very real expression of public concern. It is a widespread expression of concern.
I want to say right now that I resent an aside made earlier today by the Leader of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Oshawa. He said that we on this side preach the right to strike and then want to shut one down the moment a strike gets going. As the Leader of the New Democratic Party pointed out, it will be two weeks on Monday since this strike has been crippling the nation.
The principle of the right to strike in the public service is one thing. It is an arguable principle for some of us on this side, but it is now an accepted fact of life. A prolonged strike in such an essential public service as the Post Office is quite something else again. And we, as elected representatives, feel we should do whatever we can on behalf of the hundreds of thousands of Canadians affected by this strike. They may not care about the niceties and technicalities or the crucial aspects of whether one more body is added to the negotiating table. We think it is up to this House of Commons to get that strike stopped in the absence of successful negotiations at the table. I share the hope of my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that maybe there will be some hope of getting the parties back to the negotiating table and getting a negotiated settlement. I repeat, if we do not have that negotiated settlement, it is up to this House of Commons to get this strike stopped, get the mails flowing again and to get into place some mechanism, some way of reconciling the right to strike with the chaos that results when the whole country is held up for ransom by the disruption of an essential public service.
I believe we have to think through very carefully about what services are essential in this society. But even our friends to the left cannot deny that the Post Office and the movement of mail is indeed a vitally essential public service and worthy of the concern of this Parliament before we take a three-month holiday. My opinion is shared by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. All members of Parliament receive copies of Mandate. We all take this group of businessmen seriously. The federation plea is "end the chaos". In one of its publications we read:
We're mad. In fact federal members are seething over the public sector strikes that so badly affect the health and survival of the country's small and mediumsized enterprises.
Strike after public service strike has created chaos.
Post office unions are among the worst offenders, but the strike, go-slow, work-to-rule mentality has, over time, tied up everything from airlines to police protection services.
In my view, the Mandate article has real credibility. The federation makes a very strong case about what happens to
July 10, 1981

strikes in any part of the public service, but especially in the Post Office. As I said, 1 think it would be unconscionable for this Parliament to adjourn for the summer without coming up with some form of legislation recommending some solution to end this strike in the absence of negotiation.
People keep talking about bad faith being shown on both sides of the postal dispute. But the ultimate act of bad faith would be shown by the Parliament of Canada to the people of this country if we were to take our three-month holiday and leave this nation in the grip of a postal union whose actions are crippling the country and causing all sorts of economic hardships to the people of Canada.
My leader touched on the costs of the 1975 mail strike and what that could mean in 1981 dollar terms. The 1975 strike lasted 42 days. According to the Canadian Direct Mail Marketing Association, the expected loss to the Canadian economy for a 1981 postal strike of the same timing and duration as the 1975 strike is $407.6 million, which amounts to $9.7 million per day.
Reference was made earlier to Mary McMaster's pottery operation in my home town of Dundas, Ontario. That pottery business is a small business with 21 employees. Mrs. McMas-ter has closed down her plant for the rest of the summer, laying off 21 people because she cannot receive incoming orders or accounts and she cannot do her billing. Understandably, Mrs. McMaster is fed up with the Post Office. She is fed up with the strikes and the salaries disputes. In fact, she is fed up with the whole civil service. Mrs. MacMaster feels, and she is just one of many hundreds of thousands of Canadians expressing this view, that it is totally irresponsible for this Parliament to recess during the postal strike, abandoning thousands of small business owners to deal with this colossal problem on their own. Having talked to Mary McMaster myself, I know what a problem this will be for her because having laid off these 21 employees, it will take her months to gear everything up again. There are many thousands of businesses which are like Mary McMaster's.
People on the government side who are trying to duck this issue and run away from it ask what positive proposal we have on this side. I would suggest that perhaps we return to the idea of a public interest disputes commission. This proposal was made by the former postmaster general, the hon. member for Vancouver South, when the Conservative government was in power. He said:
It is recognized that sometimes the private right to strike or lockout must give way to the larger public right to receive essential services, whether those services are provided in the public or the private sector.
In order to help prevent recourse to strikes affecting essential services, the Progressive Conservative Party advocates the establishment of a public interest disputes commission. This was first recommended in 1968 by Dean H. D. Woods and others who made up the federally appointed Task Force on Canadian Industrial Relations. The Task Force Report said:
"The public has an interest in being protected from the hardship caused by work stoppages which interrupt the supply of essential goods and services."
Summer Recess
However, while some services are easily defined in advance as "essential" a strike can have effects under some circumstances that are not easily anticipated.
Again, I come back to Mary McMaster and the 21 employees that she had to lay off about 48 hours ago.
The Woods report listed seven factors that should be considered in finding solutions to essential service disputes. Because labour relations are not nearly as simple as some believe, these factors need to be understood and are set out exactly as they appear in the report. I will not take the time to read that report into the record. It may be found elsewhere in Hansard. But a public interest disputes commission would be a new approach, a better management-labour climate in both the public and the private sectors. The report states that new approaches are working in other jurisdictions and, where compatible, experience gained in these other areas may well be incorporated along with the Woods report suggestions.
We on this side have said we will consult with labour and management and prepare legislation for introduction to Parliament once we become the Government of Canada again. This is an idea which we are dusting off, but it is an important one. Labour and management relations are essentially a matter of human relations. Just passing more laws is not the answer. We believe that the public interests disputes commission is a step toward establishing a more effective framework for the settlement of legitimate issues. It could serve to minimize work stoppages in essential services.
In closing these brief remarks, I would like to reiterate that this Parliament and we as elected representatives have a right and a duty to speak on behalf of the Canadian people. We want to ensure that we are representing their best interests. Their best interests right now are served by getting the mail going again. However the mail gets going, whether it is through a negotiated settlement or Parliament legislating the CUPW workers back to work, we will not know until after the weekend. However, in the final analysis, we the representatives in this institution are responsible to the Canadian people to keep one of the most essential and fundamental Canadian services going. That is Her Majesty's Royal Mail, Canada's post office. That is why we feel it would be dead wrong for this House to rise this afternoon leaving the country in the grips of this crippling and very unfortunate postal strike.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to discuss the matter of the adjournment of this House which has been brought forward by the President of the Privy Council. During his remarks, he explained in a glorious fashion how his government had 61 bills passed through this House.
Sixty-five.

Sixty-five, 103. I wish to state unequivocally that I could not agree with at least 66 per cent of those bills. They will destroy the economy of Canada and take away the rights of Canadian citizens. They are bills which will expropriate the property of Canadians. The government has not accomplished very much since the session began in April, 1980.

July 10, 1981
Summer Recess
The postal strike is very critical. It is hurting every person in this country. The large corporations need not worry, just the little guys who cannot collect the dollars. The banks will extend them money. With interest rates at 22 per cent, I can understand why a bank would be delighted to extend credit. We are not looking after the people of this country.
Concerns have been raised in this House about blood samples getting to hospitals. There are many examples of how this strike is destroying Canada just as much as the legislation that has been passed in this session. I support the Leader of the Opposition in his belief that we should stay here in order to give a message to the Canadian public that the government and the unions should get their act together and resolve this matter. I do not say we should necessarily give in to the union because this new round of wage increases will result in increased inflation. It is all we have seen in this House in this last session.
When they sit down at the table, the government blames the union and the union blames the government. Now they are all blaming Mike Warren who is being brought in as an extra. They cannot even do their own work without bringing in somebody who has not even started his job. He is to be chief executive officer of a corporation which has not yet been formed. If he can do it, that is great and I will give him credit. He may be successful. He has had a good deal of experience with a Conservative government in a part of this country. Perhaps a Conservative civil servant will be able to help out.
I would like to refer to some of the things the government has not accomplished and to which I take objection. This is the year of the handicapped. I attempted to move a motion under Standing Order 43 and raised a question in this House. I also wrote to the Minister of State for Finance asking for some relief for the handicapped people of this country who must use braces but are not in wheelchairs. I received the most ridiculous answer from the minister. Six weeks ago I wrote him a second letter, but I have not yet received an answer. This is why I complain that we should not be going home for a holiday until we accomplish what we have set out to do.
This is the year of the disabled. If the government were to protect one segment of our society, it could have been the handicapped. I came upon a situation where a gentleman suffered through 36 hours in the Toronto-Dominion Centre. They did not give a damn about him. That is exactly how this government feels about the citizens of this country who are affected by the mail not getting through. The only ones to gain will be the banks. The large oil companies will not suffer but the smaller ones will. They will not be able to get their working agreements with other companies through the mail.
Maybe it is time to look philosophically at the Post Office. Maybe the government's opinion is that if we leave them out long enough, the private sector may pick up. That is fine for those businesses and individuals who can afford it. However, we must address the situation of senior citizens who will not receive their cheques, as well as needy Canadians such as the handicapped who are not capable of going to government
offices to pick up cheques. We must look after the unemployed who are out of work as a result of the poor economic policies of this government. To say they can stay out for two years and the private sector will look after them will not work. It will destroy small business and many individuals.
This government boasts about its great legislation. I would like to refer to one of the great pieces of legislation of all time, the National Energy Program. It has brought this country to its knees. I hope Lalonde and Leitch are using the federal express to correspond with each other.
Recently I had an opportunity to visit western Canada where I met with small service operators. It is not only those in the west who are going into bankruptcy. This is hurting every segment of industry in Ontario. When you bring the industrial heartland to its knees, you create a chaos from which this country cannot recover. Much as I would like to be lying beside my swimming pool or playing tennis, I would be willing to stay here till hell freezes over, and perhaps this place is the closest we will come to that, or at least stay here until next winter in order to try to get something moving.

The House resumed, from Monday, June 2, 1980, consideration of the motion of Mr. Knowles:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to provide for the pensions payable under these two acts to be available at age 60 to all persons who meet the other requirements of the said acts and who are not in or are prepared to withdraw from the labour market, and also to provide for the basic amount of the pension payable under the Old Age Security Act, at age 60 for those not in the labour market and to everyone at age 65, to be increased to $400 per month, for this basic amount to be escalated each year by an amount that will enable pensioners not only to keep up with rising living costs but to share in rising standards, and also to provide for the elimination of any means or income test from the Old Age Security Act, so that the full pension thereunder will be recognized as the established right of all our people.
July 10, 1981

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED LOWERING OF AGE ELIGIBILITY AND INCREASE IN MONTHLY BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an interesting motion which was last debated on June 2, 1980. It is a rather lengthy motion which includes more than one idea. The motion would provide for the payment of pensions at the age of 60 to all persons who are not in the labour market or who are prepared to withdraw from it. It would also provide for an increase in the old age security payment, that is, the basic payment as opposed to the increases that the Liberal government has recently given in the supplement. While I am sure the concern on all parts of the House is equal for people who are finding it difficult to manage on a fixed income, the different philosophies of the different political parties would, of course, suggest different approaches. Retirement at age 60 is something which is also being proposed now, I understand, by the newly elected socialist government of France, partly as an answer to the question of youth unemployment. Its slogan, I believe, goes something like: "Less work so that everybody works".
The approach includes not only early retirement, but also a shortening of the work week. This, of course, is one approach to youth unemployment, but we will have to watch it with some interest to see if, in fact, it proves to be effective because the jobs which are vacated by 60-year old experienced workers are not necessarily the jobs which will be suitable for 20-year-old or 18-year-old persons who are unskilled and inexperienced.
The other aspect, of course, is the problem of income maintenance for older people. This is very real. We all know that the poorest people in Canada at the present time are older women who have not been in the labour force long enough to have acquired pension credits. Women generally have interrupted careers and work at the kinds of jobs which do not carry private pension plans. In any case, the private pension plans in Canada have generally not served their members well. But whether increasing the old age security for everyone and making it available after age 60 is going to answer this, or is the best way to answer it, I think is very much open to debate.
The hon. member's motion would also eliminate any means test. The Liberal party's position has been to try to assist first those who most need assistance. Therefore, we have opted to increase the old age supplement, that is, the part of income maintenance which is means tested. We have increased this, and we will try to manage further increases for those people who are clearly in need of assistance. We would give a much lower priority to increasing the old age security, that is, the basic part of the plan which is paid to everyone, whether they need it or not, and whether they are wealthy or poor.
The fact that we would put the first emphasis on increasing the supplement rather than on the basic part of the pension does not, of course, alter the fact that we know that pensions, generally, in Canada are greatly in need of improvement. The Committee which was so ably chaired by Senator Croll produced some very interesting figures, and also a number of
Old Age Security
different solutions which I think should be looked at with at least as much attention as the particular solution advanced by the hon. member in this motion. That particular report suggested widening the eligibility of people to pay into the Canada Pension Plan, increasing the contributions, with the aim of everyone receiving more substantial Canada Pension Plan at the end of a career.
In terms of the question of retirement at the age of 60, this again is perhaps a question where one would like to see considerably more flexibility. Again, the report of the committee which was chaired by Senator Croll does, in fact, suggest flexible retirement ages because clearly there are many people who wish to work long after the age of 60 and are very capable of doing so. Increasingly, people are not only living longer but are also remaining healthy and active longer. On the other hand, there are people, particularly people who have done hard manual work, who are tired and who might wish to retire at age 60 or even earlier.
In my own constituency, I find that many people are having great difficulty in working, even by their mid-fifties, people who have worked very hard at backbreaking work in construction who have perhaps had an accident or two. People who, although intelligent, have not had the opportunity to upgrade their qualifications can find themselves at a very distinct disadvantage in the labour force long before the age of sixty. Indeed, I would like to see, as a higher priority, some special plans for people in that age group, for the older construction worker who is tired but who, once his physical strength has gone, is finding it very difficult to acquire the skills which would let him move into another type of job.
There was another aspect of the hon. member's motion which also gives me pause. The suggestion in the hon. member's motion that old age security for everyone be increased at age 60 without a means test, would mean a substantial cost. If that cost appreciably improves the lot of Canadians, then of course I would not quarrel with it because there are certain costs which have to be met in terms of social justice and humanity. However, as I think of the number of working poor, the number of families where one parent or both work very hard because they have a large family, and as I think of the needs of poor children in our society, I wonder if the shift of revenues toward older people and away from young people is necessarily in the best interest of society. My own preference would be for something in the nature of a guaranteed annual income, something which assists people of every age, whether employed or not, to have a standard of living which meets what most of us would consider to be a decent standard and which allows them to raise their children and educate their children-if they still have children of that age-without undue stress on both parents. We are increasingly seeing families with parents who are thoughtful and caring and who have much to give to their children, but are obliged to work such long hours that they spend little time with them. Something in the nature of a guaranteed annual income-one can call it by what name one would choose-it seems to me would meet the needs of both older people who need income supple-

July 10, 1981
Old Age Security
ments and also the needs of some of these young parents who are struggling to give their children a healthy lifestyle and exhausting themselves in the process.
In closing, I would like to say that, while I appreciate and respect the concern about poverty among older people which is shown by the hon. member's motion, I would rather see an approach which would assist all poor people in Canada to use their own resources and to have the kind of equality of opportunity we would like everyone to have, whether young or old.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED LOWERING OF AGE ELIGIBILITY AND INCREASE IN MONTHLY BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too rise to speak in the debate on the motion put forward last June 2, 1980 by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). It is a great honour to speak to this motion presented by a person who has fought so hard for so many years for older people in Canada.
As the last speaker mentioned, the motion concerns amendments to the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan. Although we are pleased to have this matter brought forward today, it is interesting that for some rather mysterious reason it is brought forward after last evening when members of Parliament voted themselves a generous pay increase. I think many of us recall the speeches made and the pleas made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre last night on behalf of senior citizens across our land. I hope this bodes well for pensioners today and that there will be unanimous agreement on this motion, although I cannot help but comment that we have fewer than one dozen members of Parliament sitting listening to the debate on this motion on a Friday afternoon.
The motion put by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre over one year ago includes a number of points which I will quickly review. The motion concerns old age security and the guaranteed income supplement, as well as the Canada Pension Plan. In his motion the hon. member recommends that these plans should be available at age 60. It should not be for everyone but for those who are not in the labour market or those who choose-and they should have the right to choose- at age 60 to retire. They should have the assurance that they have adequate incomes on which to survive.
In his speech last year the hon. member pointed out that this also would make many more jobs available for young people in a rapidly tightening market situation. This, of course, is not the main reason for the proposal, and we hasten to point out that we would support the flexible retirement plans suggested by Senator Croll which would allow people to choose at age 60 either to work or to retire with adequate pensions as a right and not just as a token welfare gesture.
The motion also recommends increasing the old age pension to $400 for those aged 60 who are not working and for all people at age 65, the age upon which our universal old age pension is based.
The motion also recommends that the Canadian Pension Plan be reviewed and be changed so that it is available at age 60. This would make a consistent policy for all older people.
I think we should note also that the motion mentions several points which in effect are goals that we in the New Democratic Party would say are important goals for pensions and for older people. We should eliminate the means or income test so that pensions are a right and not offered as a matter of charity. We would see implicit in this that there must be tax reforms which would ensure that wealthy people receiving these pensions would be taxed back and that that money would go into the kitty in order to make this a universal and equitable plan.
I would like to make a personal reference. I have a neighbour next door whose name is Buster, a man in his eighties who never lets me forget the needs of senior citizens, just as my hon. colleague does not.

speechtext: Good for Buster.

speechtext:
Because of him I could not vote on the bill last night, although I acknowledge that it is needed and certainly is just from the point of view of the work of members of Parliament. If Buster had been here yesterday, he would have been demonstrating outside, just as my colleague was demonstrating inside. He would have been fighting, not against pay for the very hard work members of Parliament do, but for a fair and adequate guaranteed income for the pioneers of our land.
Buster is typical of many west coast pioneers. He came from Ontario to the prairies when he was a young man. He worked on the prairies before the depression in days when things were very difficult. Then he moved to British Columbia. He worked in remote areas of the north. As a mechanic he repaired ships and often travelled up and down the British Columbia coast, stopping in at Indian villages and so forth. During the war he kept ships in repair. He worked hard to keep our navy in the state of repair which was needed. However, of all the experiences in his lifetime, this man will never forget the shame and indignity during the depression years. This pioneer was proud of his independence and worked hard all his life. He will never forget the indignity of having to ask for welfare to support his young family at a certain period during the depression. As we do, he believes that an old age pension and a guaranteed adequate income should be a right and that it should never, never be a charity for which people must beg or suffer indignity.
What is happening to our senior citizens today? In one's year time things are worse, not better. Granted, the Liberals fulfilled their one single token election promise and brought forward an extra $35 a month for senior citizens, but even with indexing this still leaves single senior citizens far below the poverty line, the poverty line for a single person being recognized as $5,500.
July 10, 1981

So even if we pass the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the combined old age pension and GIS will total only $4,800 per year, still below the poverty line. It is a year later and we should probably be going for more than a $400 increase. The cost of living for every senior citizen and every person aged 60 has gone up phenomenally in one year. Rents for the average older person in Vancouver are now far in excess of 60 per cent of their income. The cost of food is more than double. Fuel costs are up, and we have no cost of living supplement to help people in that regard. Taxes for those who own their own homes are up. Of course, we have extreme variations in the cost of living across Canada.
I put in a plea as well for increased pensions. We should also have shelter allowances, particularly to help older people faced with exorbitant costs of shelter, whether it be their own home or rental accommodation. We certainly must have pensions increased to at least $400 a month. If you think of your own parents or friends in the 60 year old age group, with the changing employment situation and the fact that as people get older they have to retrain or be forced out of the labour force, surely it is reasonable to give people a choice at that age of whether to continue in the work force or to retire with dignity.
I would like to speak for a moment to the pensions, which do not at all provide for the needs of women. My friend and colleague mentioned this in his speech last year, and many times since then. We know the system discriminates against women, particularly those in that very important class of workers, the homemakers and parents raising children. They are in effect raising the new generation. Many of our women now reaching 40, 50 and 60 years of age have worked very hard in raising their families. In the case of women on the farm, for example, they have carried on another full-time job as well. In recent years, of course, they have worked in industrial areas and in the community, as well as in the home.
Now, if we could just think a moment about the working conditions of the homemakers. Their job requires long hours, particularly when children are younger. They have no control over the working hours and they work seven days a week. They have no pensions, no benefits and no holidays because even on their holidays they usually go off with their families and do the same things they do at home, only under more difficult circumstances. In essence, they are workers in a most terrible and deplorable situation, yet they have no financial compensation. They have no cheque coming in that they can consider their own, that they can go and spend, probably on the family, but at least something they can decide to spend in their own right. They have no money to pay into the Canada Pension Plan, which brings us back to this motion. It is really very important that we begin to look at how this group of workers can have some form of income. We have some proposals on that which I will perhaps speak to another day, which will give them an allowance and give them the choice of working outside the home when children are younger, and thereby enable them to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan.
Old Age Security
In British Columbia over the past year the New Democratic Party sponsored a task force on older women. We travelled to many parts of British Columbia, remote areas in the interior as well as the larger metropolitan areas. We spoke to many women in their middle and older years and those who work with and are concerned about women in that age group. Without exception, every group presenting briefs, every man or woman who spoke on the situation, stressed that we in Canada have to change the pension system so that women who are likely to be unemployed in their 50s or 60s, if not earlier, have a decent guaranteed income. In addition, they should have decent pensions to protect them as they get older.
We are pleased, of course, that the bill concerning widows went through yesterday. That is one step, but it is not enough. We have to have adequate pensions for everyone, but particularly for women and particularly at age 60. The Liberal party-and I am sorry all the representatives of the Liberal party left the House during this discussion on pensions, which I hope is in the record.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the House for giving me the opportunity. I suggest that the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) is really drawing a long bow if he suggests that the provision against discrimination with respect to age means we have to pay family allowances regardless of age. Do we pay them to people as old as I am, or do we pay old age pensions to people as young as he is? subsubtopic: SUGGESTED LOWERING OF AGE ELIGIBILITY AND INCREASE IN MONTHLY BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to hear some of the many different views held by various members of the House on the topic of retirement and benefits for the retired. I am especially glad to have the chance to make some comments on this very timely issue.
Hon. members have spent a fair bit of time discussing the many facets of retirement. In particular, they have discussed the present motion and its ancestors which entail making retirement benefits available at age 60 for those not in the labour market. I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is not advocating that all Canadians must or should cease paid employment immediately upon attaining 60 years of age. What I find particularly interesting is that we have two schools of thought on the issue of retirement age: one supporting a longer working career and the other a considerably shorter one. Could this be a reflection of an ambivalence toward working and retirement being felt by the Canadian population? I believe this must be so. It would be all too easy to dismiss this social phenomenon as an indication that people simply do not know what they want. On
the contrary, it seems to be a very real and important demonstration that the Canadian public is not just simply a faceless mass moving uniformly in one direction. Rather, in this age of awareness Canadians are coming to the natural realization that different people have different needs and expectations. For some, their lifetime fulfilment and objectives are met in their work world. They want, are capable of, and very much need this continued contact. For others, their lives are not motivated by a need to work in paid employment. They find the important qualities in their lives outside the labour market. Each approach to living is equally valid. Our vigil will be long-enduring if we intend to wait until the Canadian population reaches a consensus on such an individual and personalized matter as retirement and optimum retirement ages. A final distillation of views may never materialize.
How can we as legislators best respond to a situation where there is no clearcut right and wrong, where in fact what is right for one might be entirely wrong for another? The only reasonable course to follow is one which will provide the maximum amount of flexibility, one which allows Canadians to have as much access as possible to the greatest number of options.
It might be worthwhile at this point to examine the development of our present retirement system. Not so many years ago the Canadian public was coping with almost the entire responsibility for providing for its income needs after retirement from the work force. As recently as 1965, the income guaranteed to a retired Canadian by the Government of Canada was only $75 per month, payable at age 70 under the Old Age Security Act. Some were lucky and were able to participate in an employer-sponsored pension plan, but others were not so fortunate and had to provide from their own resources and savings. Some simply could never afford to retire and were obliged to continue working. Since then some dramatic improvements have been made in retirement benefits for the elderly.
In 1966, the retirement age for old age security began to be reduced a year at a time until it reached the present OAS retirement age of 65 in 1970. Also in 1966 the Canada Pension Plan came into effect. A compulsory, contributory pension plan, the CPP provides coverage to virtually every Canadian wage earner and has become increasingly important as a source of present and future retirement income.
Parliamentarians did not intend that these two programs would provide all the retirement income Canadians might wish to have. Rather, the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act were seen as providing the foundation of a layered retirement system. The first level, the flat rate old age security pension, provides a base upon which the second level, the earnings-related Canada and Quebec Pension Plan benefits, is built. Together with the guaranteed income supplement, these benefits ensure a minimum amount of income which adequately provides for the basic needs of retired Canadians. There is still ample room for Canadians to apply their initiative and supplement this minimum amount, because the third level of the system is the additional income available through private pension plans, registered retirement savings
July 10, 1981

plans, investments or other sources which can be seen as providing whatever supplementary margin of comfort the individual might require.
This retirement system gives Canadian workers a great deal of flexibility in determining when they will retire. First, there is no federal statute legally requiring the retirement of each and every Canadian at a specified age. Benefits are available at age 65 under both the OAS program and the CPP, but neither stipulates that in order to receive benefits the individual must be retired or removed from the active labour force.
A wide array of retirement options is available to Canadians. Almost two million Canadians have taken advantage of the tax savings and the wide range of choice allowed in setting up registered retirement savings plans. When the time comes to turn their savings into retirement income, taxpayers can either invest their RRSP proceeds in a life annuity with an insurance company prior to reaching 71 years of age, or withdraw the funds in a lump sum and pay income tax on this amount in the same year. Two additional alternatives increase flexibility while retaining the basic principle that RRSP funds are for retirement income. The first alternative allowed the purchase of a fixed term annuity to provide benefits to age 90. The second alternative allowed taxpayers to have RRSP savings placed in an investment vehicle known as a registered retirement income fund. The transfer of an RRSP into any of the retirement income options can occur at any time between age 60 and age 71. These alternatives provide a range of choice available to Canadians in planning for their retirement.
The motion before us today is not new to the House. This is not the first time the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has proposed this motion. If the hon. member's tenacity in the past is an example of what is to come, it will probably not be the last time.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
But I think there is a very real danger in over legislating. Governments have been accused of this tactic in the past. It is time we all recognized that it is nearly impossible to devise a plan with universal applicability which, at the same time, has the capability of adapting to individual needs. Perhaps it is better to have a straightforward basic plan which is fairly simple to administer and from which the individual, if he or she wants, can build to develop a personalized retirement package.
The issue of retirement age has been debated in this House on many occasions, as I have said, and that in itself is evidence of our concern and desire to explore the various approaches to retirement. As our elderly population continues to grow, the age of retirement becomes more and more relevant, both in economic and in social terms.
What have elderly Canadians a right to expect? Canadians have traditionally believed not only in the right to work but in the right to work for as long as they wished, or were able to. Hon. members will agree that as a fundamental right senior
Old Age Security
Canadians should have the right to make reasonable personal choices. It follows then that we must retain a retirement income system in this country which makes some provisions for individual options.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on the point raised by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes). This is one of the points which concerned me, and probably others, with regard to the Constitution wherein it is said that there is no discrimination because of age. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre expressed the hope that there would be no discrimination because of age. The difficutly is that when this provision is written into the charter of rights, if the judges decide that is the case, then our hands are tied. This is one of the very dangerous points of that type of legislation if left to the judges to decide and not to the legislators of our country. If some decision needs to be made without it being tied into the charter, individuals could come to their members of Parliament and members of their legislatures and the matter could be brought before the government of the day which could see that justice was done. But if a decision is given by the Supreme Court of Canada, then our hands are tied until the Constitution is changed. I hope that is one of the reasons why the Supreme Court judges will throw it out.
The next point I would like to mention is that social legislation is important in any country. The party to which 1 belong is very conscious of the importance of social legislation. I think probably every party in Canada has its own social legislation program. I personally feel that social legislation should be written in such a way that our people generally come under that legislation. That is why I question the social legislation which is now included in the negotiation package of our postal service which is presently on strike. They are asking for a maternity package. If it is granted, then one particular group will have better maternity benefits than any other group in Canada, including those on unemployment insurance. Thus,

July 10, 1981
Old Age Security
differences begin to build up between women. Some receive a certain amount of money under one program and some another amount of money under a different program, and others still receive nothing because they come under no program. I feel that social legislation should be enacted by the governments of the day, nationally by the federal government and, to the extent they can, by provincial governments. This would allow all women to come within a similar category for similar benefits. This is my view. I object to including maternity benefits in a negotiation package for just one small group. I believe in maternity benefits. As a matter of fact, I was part of the legislation in Alberta which led the way with regard to maternity benefits several years ago. I believe that course was followed by other governments later. The fact that babies were to be born in hospitals and not in some other places saved the lives of hundreds of babies born during the depression years.
Something else which always appalls me about social legislation, and which causes me great difficulty when explaining it to the people who come to me, is where there are differences between two women on one street, for example. Both are widows; one is 62 years of age and the other is 64. Neither one's spouse came under the old age pension but the spouse of one had contributed to the Canada Pension Plan and the spouse of the other had not, for the simple reason that he was not working during the period of 1976, or because he was working in a field in which that pension was not deducted. Both these women came to see me at the same time. They told me they had come to me to see whether they could receive the Canada pension. I asked them if their husbands had contributed to the plan. As I said before, one husband had and the other had not. Neither of the two women had contributed since they were housewives. I was able to tell one of the ladies that she qualified for a certain amount of Canada pension and that I would be glad to fill in the application for her. I told the other lady that it was no use because she had never contributed. She said that she had no opportunity to contribute, nor had her husband. I recognize that, but they receive no Canada pension.
This type of social legislation where we make differences of flesh of one and fish of another does not lead to a good feeling among our people. In my view, our social legislation should be overhauled with a view to giving the benefits to all those who fall within that group.
I recall that when I was first campaigning for the House of Commons in 1979 I knocked at a door in a small town. When the lady came to the door, I introduced myself. She said that she wanted to talk to me, and also to every other candidate, but so far I was the only one who had knocked at her door. She said she wanted to contribute to the Canada pension and that she was a housewife. I do not believe she had a husband, I guess she was a single woman. I did not go into all the details of her life. She said that she was able to contribute and that she should have the right to contribute. I rather agree with that. The women who are spending their lives in the kitchen and who are raising children, who are doing one of the most important jobs in the nation, should have the right to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan. If that legislation were so amended that would be fine.
There is still another group, however, those who will not be able to contribute. When people get to the age where they need help, are we going to treat them on the basis of whether they did or did not contribute to the plan? I think that is an important point. People of an advanced age who need help should get it, and that is where I differ somewhat, not too much, from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on the matter of universality.
I know people who are aged 66, 70 or 75 today who are well off and are drawing the old age pension. They have plenty to get by on and do not need it but as there is universality, they are entitled to it under the law. Personally, I question that.
Universality sounds fine and at one time I advocated it but when we see what social legislation is costing the nation, and when we consider that many people get nothing, then I think we have to reassess the situation. We must ask if those who are well off and have made provision for their senior years and are not going to suffer in any way, should draw this allowance while other people in the age bracket who need it badly, get nothing.
I think of single women between the ages of 60 and 65. If a woman's husband was a pensioner and she was on spouse's allowance, she is fortunate, because the legislation that the Clark government introduced to continue that pension for the spouse filled one gap. A lot of women did not have a husband who was a pensioner and indeed, some did not have a husband at all. I know one woman who spent her life looking after a disabled sister. She has no way of getting help, except through welfare. An hon. member from British Columbia told us that some people who have been independent all their lives are reluctant to go to the welfare office. I think the welfare office has its place, Mr. Speaker, and I do not look down on anyone who has to go there. It is there to help people, but in spite of anything we say, many people feel that there is a disgrace in applying for welfare.
I think we made a mistake in our social legislation when we did away with the disability pension. There is a disability pension today if one has contributed to the Canada Pension Plan but a lot of people did not and are now dependent on welfare. They should be in a different category. At one time there were two disability pension plans, the federal and the provincial-at least the province of Alberta had a plan and I suppose other provinces did as well. At present the only disability pension is paid under the Canada Pension Plan. In many cases the only redress for the disabled is to seek help through welfare, and that is not satisfactory.
I think the government realizes that a lot of work has to be done on pensions. The Canada Pension Plan does not do the complete job and that is aggravated by the pension bill passed in this House last night for MPs and senators. They can now draw a full pension at age 35 if elected at age 20, based on the best six years of earning. That is pretty rich, when someone
July 10, 1981

can draw a pension for life at age 35, or 40 or 45, when they are still in good health.
1 think we have to inject some sense into this, Mr. Speaker. Surely pensions should be paid as the result of a number of years of service and contributions. Even if the pensioner has contributed part of it, someone else has paid the other part. I think this type of pension should be reassessed.
With regard to the Old Age Security payment at age 65, one of the things we can do is change the compulsory retirement age in many industries and services from 65 to at least 70. Even 70 may be questioned if a person is well and able. I know of people working on farms today almost as hard as they did 20 years ago and they are now aged 71 and 72.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED LOWERING OF AGE ELIGIBILITY AND INCREASE IN MONTHLY BENEFITS
speechtext: Some people of 70 still play a great game of hockey!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED LOWERING OF AGE ELIGIBILITY AND INCREASE IN MONTHLY BENEFITS
speechtext:
I don't know about that. These people are happy, Mr. Speaker. I know a chap who took early retirement-I have to talk fast, Mr. Speaker-from the Department of Highways. He was an excellent engineer but that was all he knew. When he retired, he sat in his back yard and dreamed about the bridges and roads he had built. He just lasted two years. He took retirement at age 61 but he had nothing to do then. He had worked hard all his life and suddenly he found there was nothing to live for. That is a real danger.
We all like social legislation, Mr. Speaker. Someone made the point that lowering the age to 60 for those who are not in the labour market or who are prepared to withdraw from it is a redeeming feature of the bill. I think all our social legislation needs to be reassessed so that we can help those who need help and that we do not provide pensions for those who do not need them.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, because 1 do not want to deprive my colleague of his right to speak with regard to the business of the House. We still intend to proceed on Monday with Bill C-48 but we may instead decide to resume debate on the adjournment motion started today. Probably before the end of the question period on Monday we will be able to advise the opposition parties whether we will debate the report stage
Old Age Security
of Bill C-48 or whether we will resume debate on the adjournment motion. Should 1 know before the question period, I will advise my colleagues. For the time being we intend to proceed with Bill C-48, but I must inform the House that we may instead decide to continue debating the motion to adjourn. In any event, I shall advise opposition parties before the end of the question period on Monday.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Knowles:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to provide for the pensions payable under these two acts to be available at age 60 to all persons who meet the other requirements of the said acts and who are not in or are prepared to withdraw from the labour market, and also to provide for the basic amount of the pension payable under the Old Age Security Act, at age 60 for those not in the labour market and to everyone at age 65, to be increased to $400 per month, for this basic amount to be escalated each year by an amount that will enable pensioners not only to keep up with rising living costs but to share in rising living standards, and also to provide for the elimination of any means or income test from the Old Age Security Act, so that the full pension thereunder will be recognized as the established right of all our people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED LOWERING OF AGE ELIGIBILITY AND INCREASE IN MONTHLY BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree with his motion. As Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance I have some problems with the motion. The main one is that I think that at this time the OAS represents an outlay in the range of $6 billion per year. If we were to accept the motion and make the OAS payable at age 60 and incorporate the GIS, that would mean an additional outlay of some $5 billion per year and would raise the total outlay for the program to $11 billion, or nearly doubling the cost for all time.
